readerTitle: Your startup hit 100 people. Your org chart is still from 20.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (급여 소프트웨어·온보딩 서비스 스타트업, 케이터링 스타트업) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 100명 규모의 조직 설계는 두 가지 질문으로 정리된다. 무엇을 기준으로 팀을 묶을지(기능 vs 사업부), 그리고 각 관리자가 몇 명을 맡고 몇 단계를 둘지(관리 폭과 계층)다.
misconception: 회사가 커지면 큰 회사의 조직도를 그대로 가져오거나, 고객군마다 사업부를 나누는 것이 자연스러운 다음 단계다.

sources.text: 조직 설계의 표준 개념 (기능별·사업부별 조직, 관리 폭과 계층)
모든 수치와 회사는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 가상 스타트업 인원 구성: 엔지니어 30 + 온보딩·지원 35 + 영업 20 + 기타 15 = 100명.
재설계 조직도 계산: 창업자 1 + 부문장 6 + 팀장 10 + 실무자 83 = 100명. 팀장 1명당 약 8명(83 ÷ 10 = 8.3). 창업자의 직속 보고자 14명 → 6명. 부문장이 팀장 1~3명과 일부 실무자를 직접 맡는다는 가정입니다.
관리 폭(한 관리자가 맡는 인원)의 적정 수치는 업무 성격에 따라 크게 다르며 보편적 정답이 없습니다. 카드에는 특정 연구 수치를 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Your startup hit 100 people. Your org chart is still from 20.
body: Monday, 9 a.m. The founder of a payroll software startup opens her calendar. Fourteen one-on-ones this week. Fourteen people report straight to her.
A sales rep waits two days for her answer on a discount. A support lead waits for a hiring yes. The company grew five times. The org chart didn't change.

image.label: A founder's calendar packed with one-on-ones
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 책상 위 노트북 화면에 일주일 캘린더가 빈틈없이 "1:1" 블록으로 가득 참. 창업자 뒤로 작은 사람 인형들이 줄을 서서 기다림. 실제 앱 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Split into divisions, or keep functions?
body: The startup sells one payroll product plus setup help to small businesses. Its 100 people: 30 engineers, 35 onboarding and support staff, 20 in sales, 15 in finance and admin.
New customers stall between sales and onboarding. The founder wonders about splitting into two divisions: restaurants and retail. What do you do?

options.text: Split into two customer divisions, each with its own engineers, sales and support
options.feedback: *Functional vs divisional:* divisions pay off when customer groups need different products. Here you'd split 30 engineers across one codebase and copy every scarce role twice.

options.text: Keep teams by function, and make one person own the whole new-customer journey across them
options.feedback: *Functional vs divisional:* one product means shared skill is worth more than separate units. An owner fixes the handoff without splitting the company.

options.text: Keep teams by function and add a weekly meeting of all team heads to sort out handoffs
options.feedback: The meeting surfaces problems, but no one owns them. Stalled customers still end up on the founder's desk.

cards.title: Group people by what the strategy needs.
body: A **functional** structure groups people by skill: all engineers together, all support together. It builds depth and avoids duplicate roles. Its weak spot is the gaps between teams.
A **divisional** structure groups people by customer, product or place. Each unit moves fast, but it copies roles and splits expertise.
With one product and one kind of customer, the startup's problem is a gap between teams, not a need for separate businesses. So it keeps functions and closes the gap.

cards.title: Fourteen people report to the founder.
body: Decisions queue up behind her. She wants fewer direct reports without slowing the company down. Which plan fits?

options.text: Hire a COO and have all 14 report to that person instead
options.feedback: *Spans and layers:* this frees the founder, but only moves the overload one box down. The COO now has a span of 14 plus a new layer.

options.text: Name 6 function heads; each manages a few team leads of about 8 people
options.feedback: *Spans and layers:* the founder's span drops to 6, and each lead can coach a team of 8. One extra layer, used where it carries real weight.

options.text: Hire 5 senior VPs from big companies, each with 2 or 3 managers under them
options.feedback: *Spans and layers:* narrow spans stack up layers fast. Every decision climbs more steps, and you pay for managers who barely manage.

cards.title: Same 100 people, shorter queues.

breakdown.label: Function heads
breakdown.detail: Sales, onboarding, support, engineering, product, finance

breakdown.label: Frontline
breakdown.detail: Two steps from a decision, not one long queue

cards.callout: The goal isn't a pretty chart. It's that most decisions get made close to the work.
cards.softwareNote: In software teams, spans often differ by function. Support teams doing similar work can run wider; engineering teams with complex, varied work often need narrower spans and more senior leads.

cards.title: A new chart is a cost, not a cure.
body: Every structure change moves people's bosses, habits and loyalties. Expect weeks of slower work while new leads find their feet.
Don't promote your best individual workers into team leads by default. Leading 8 people is a different job.
And plan to look again. A structure that fits 100 people may strain at 200, especially if the strategy changes, such as launching a second product.

cards.title: Now it's a catering startup.
body: A 100-person catering company runs kitchens in three cities. One city serves offices, one weddings, one hospitals. Each has its own clients and menus.
Every menu change waits for the head chef at headquarters. Clients complain about slow replies. How should you organize?

options.text: Keep one central kitchen team, sales team and delivery team across all three cities
options.feedback: *Functional vs divisional:* shared functions build skill, but these markets are very different. Every local question still climbs to headquarters.

options.text: Give each city a lead who runs its kitchen, sales and delivery; keep food safety and purchasing shared
options.feedback: *Functional vs divisional:* different customers justify divisions. Keeping safety and purchasing shared protects standards and buying power.

options.text: Make each city fully separate, with its own recipes, suppliers and safety rules
options.feedback: Each city moves fast, but you lose bulk buying and one safety standard. A single mistake can hurt all three brands.

cards.title: Decide how to group people, then how many each leader carries.
body: You used two ideas. **Functional vs divisional:** group by skill when customers need the same thing, by market when they don't. **Spans and layers:** give leaders a team they can really lead, and add layers only where they carry weight.
**Try it today:** count your direct reports and the steps between you and the frontline. Where do decisions wait longest?
